newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's top tribunal weighs questioning Gonzalez.
newsitem.headline: Spain's top tribunal weighs questioning Gonzalez.

text.p: Spanish Supreme Court judges convened on Monday to decide whether to question former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez about a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque separatist rebels in which 28 people were killed.

Gonzalez, who lost elections in March after 13 years in power, denies charges by former security chiefs and disgruntled fellow Socialists that he knew of the 1983-87 campaign of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murders by members of the security forces and hired gunmen.

His political life is at stake over Monday's decision, political commentators say. They argue that if he is called to answer questions, either as a witness or a suspect, his denials will lose credibility regardless of the final verdict.

The second chamber of the Supreme Court, which deals with cases involving members of parliament like Gonzalez, was expected to make up its mind on whether to question the ex-premier before 3 p.m. (1400 GMT), its president told a radio interviewer.
Gonzalez himself was not due to be in court for the announcement. He scheduled a news conference (1230 GMT) at Socialist Party headquarters before the expected time for the justices' statement.

Technically, the 10 judges will decide on an appeal about whether the Socialist leader should be questioned in the chief case in the covert anti-guerrilla campaign -- the kidnapping in December 1983 of Basque businessman Segundo Marey.
One of the judges, investigating justice Eduardo Moner, has already ruled that there is insufficient evidence to summon Gonzalez -- an opinion shared by state prosecutors.
The second chamber's ruling on Monday will be on an appeal against that decision, lodged by relatives of the victims.

The only new charges against Gonzalez since Moner's decision in April have come from Luis Roldan, a former Socialist head of the paramilitary Civil Guard who is accused of massive fraud and embezzlement while in office.
Roldan has testified that the illegal anti-separatist operations were official government policy and that Gonzalez was fully involved.

Gonzalez's first interior minister, Jose Barrionuevo, is already on trial at the Supreme Court on charges of masterminding and funding the shadowy death squads known as the GAL (the Spanish initials for Anti-terrorist Liberation Groups).
A senior Civil Guard general who commanded the force's main base in the Basque country is also on trial.

The conservative government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, winner of the March election, has accused Gonzalez of having waged "bodeguilla terrorism" -- a reference to a wine-cellar in his official residence where he entertained friends and hatched strategies with his closest aides.

But Aznar and his ministers, who used the "dirty war" charges to maximum effect during campaigning for the elections, have now gone back on earlier pledges and turned down court requests to declassify military files on the illegal activities.

One-third of the victims of the covert operations aimed against guerrillas of ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) were cases of mistaken identities and other errors. ETA itself has killed nearly 800 people in a fight for Basque independence which began in 1968.
